prose: Wired's Will Knight tests Flint, an open-weight 40B-parameter coding model from Recursive, Richard Socher's new company, and calls it evidence that recursive self-improvement is getting closer. Socher says the Eureka Machine automated most of the model pipeline, devising a new way to train the base model, new architectures, and silicon-specific optimized code, letting a handful of researchers build a world-class model in months; shared benchmarks show Flint beating similar-sized models on coding tasks. Knight frames the stakes: AI already helps build AI, a full loop could theoretically improve indefinitely, and that prospect is exactly what worries the doomsayers about control.
highlights: Flint: open-weight 40B coding model from Recursive
Eureka Machine automated most of development: training method, architectures, silicon-optimized code
A handful of researchers built a world-class model in months
Benchmarks show it beating similar-size models on coding

CEO Richard Socher; tested by Wired's Will Knight
